title: Boosting Inference with Guided Reasoning: Stochastic Exploration for Recursive Models
claim: Guiding stochastic exploration at inference time lifts accuracy far above the deterministic baseline, including on cases where the baseline always fails.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, annotated arrows and dashed threshold lines
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the x-axis, outer step n from 0 to about 48. The y-axis is exact-solve rate. The left panel, 'Sudoku Extreme Test Set', shows a bold red 'Guided MAP (our solution)' curve rising steeply to about 98%. Black-ringed 'Oracle particles' markers sit on top of it. Purple dots show the deterministic TRM baseline, and a dashed blue curve shows the unguided rollout. Both climb slowly to about 85%. Faint blue lines are weight-ranked particles. A dashed red vertical line at step 9 and a dashed purple horizontal line at about 87% mark where the guided method matches the baseline's final accuracy. The right panel, 'Recovery of baseline failure cases', repeats the curves with shaded bands. The baseline stays at 0%, and the red curve reaches about 86%. Gray double-headed arrows labelled 'Exploration' and 'Exploitation' split the gap between the baseline and the guided curve. The eye goes first to the red curve.
caption: Inference-time improvement on Sudoku-Extreme. Left: Our method reaches $98.0\!\pm\!0.2%$ exact-solve accuracy on the test split, improving over the deterministic TRM baseline ($85.9\!\pm\!0.6%$) and a single unguided rollout by step $10$. Right: On deterministic-failure cases, our method solves $85.9\!\pm\!1.5%$ (with $35.7\!\pm\!2.8%$ for a single unguided rollout; oracle of the guided cloud $86.0%$). Results are over $5$ seeds $\times$ $5$ folds; $\pm$ and shaded bands are the fold--seed s.d.
abstract: Recent work on recursive architectures has shown that tiny neural networks can be surprisingly powerful on structured reasoning tasks. The trick is to model reasoning trajectories with a latent dynamical system. We argue that the inference-time behaviour of these architectures is best understood as approximate inference over latent reasoning trajectories, with deterministic recursion as the one-particle, zero-noise limit. We make this view operational through guided reasoning: stochastic perturbations of the reasoning dynamics propose neighbouring trajectories, and the model's existing early-stopping head reweights them online. The framework yields three diagnostics computable from inference traces: local stability, guide alignment, with a label-free necessary condition, and cloud-token entropy. These predict whether the procedure will help and which of its outputs to trust. On Sudoku-Extreme it lifts exact-solve accuracy from $85.9\%$ to $98.0\%$ without retraining, and on PPBench, a four-type pencil-puzzle benchmark, from $62.5\%$ to $77.9\%$ with no tuning; on Maze-Hard the diagnostics flag a misaligned guide, as validation performance later confirms. The same machinery thus characterises both when recursive reasoning has room to improve at the trajectory level and when the model's internal guide can recover said improvements. Code is available at `https://github.com/digiLab-ai/bigr`.
